name: Frenotomy / tongue tie release for face

lead: A frenotomy or frenectomy releases the band of tissue under the tongue in people with tongue-tie (ankyloglossia). In appearance-focused communities it is discussed as a way to let the tongue rest against the palate, in the hope of a more defined jaw, better profile and straighter teeth.

The procedure cuts or reshapes the lingual frenulum, sometimes with a laser, to increase tongue mobility. Published research examines breastfeeding, speech and sleep outcomes; no study found tests it for changing facial structure in children or adults. The link to palate and jaw development is presented as a hypothesis.

paras: It is done as a brief clinic procedure, often followed by tongue exercises or myofunctional therapy, and people combine it with practicing tongue posture and nasal breathing. Users in these communities describe judging results over months.

Reviews describe the procedure as simple with low complication rates in infants, but case reports and a systematic review document major complications after tongue-tie release. Experts disagree about how often tongue-tie causes problems and about diagnosis, particularly of posterior tongue-tie.

angle.text: Forum posters discuss releasing the tongue frenulum so the tongue can rest against the palate, in the hope of a more defined jaw, better profile and straighter teeth. Studies cover feeding and speech outcomes rather than facial appearance.

lead: Frenotomy, also called frenectomy or frenuloplasty, is the surgical release of the lingual frenulum in people with tongue-tie (ankyloglossia). It is established for some infants with breastfeeding difficulty, and its use for speech, sleep and other outcomes is debated. [1][2]

Appearance-focused communities discuss tongue-tie release as part of a story about tongue posture and jaw development. No published human study has tested frenotomy as a way of changing facial structure. [3]

Systematic reviews report mixed evidence on speech outcomes, and a scoping review of non-infants found improvements in tongue movement with treatment, while noting that definitions and diagnostic criteria for tongue-tie are not generally agreed.
infobox: Frenotomy, frenectomy, frenuloplasty; scalpel, scissors or CO2 laser [3]

paras: Wikipedia describes ankyloglossia as a restrictive lingual frenulum that limits tongue movement, ranging from mild bands to complete tethering, with no generally accepted definition, classification or diagnostic parameters as of 2025. It reports that treatment is usually a quick frenotomy or frenuloplasty under local anesthesia, sometimes with a CO2 laser. [3]
Professionals disagree on how often tongue-tie causes symptoms. Some consider it rarely symptomatic, while others link it to many issues. [3]

sections.h: Reported links to jaw and face
paras: Wikipedia presents several associations between ankyloglossia and dental or jaw features, including open bite, a narrow high palate, tongue thrusting and temporomandibular pain, framing these as associations and hypotheses. [3] A tongue resting on the palate is described as supporting nasal breathing. [3] The article does not discuss mewing or facial aesthetics. [3]

A 2015 structured review described wide variation in reported prevalence (0.02 to 10.7%) and noted the subjectivity of the outcome measures used to judge whether tongue-tie division helps breastfeeding. [2] A 2019 review said surgical intervention should be reserved for symptomatic ankyloglossia and that frenulotomy is simple with low risk of complications. [1]

A 2024 systematic review and meta-analysis examined speech outcomes after frenectomy in children.  A 2013 systematic review looked at breastfeeding and speech articulation. [4] A 2022 scoping review of non-infants found that most treatment options significantly improved the anatomical limitation of the tongue.  A 2023 scoping review of children beyond infancy identified symptoms that may be partly attributable to ankyloglossia.  Wikipedia notes later reviews arguing speech sound development is not affected. [3]

No studies found that examine frenotomy or tongue-tie release for facial appearance or jaw structure. Studies of tongue-tie release address breastfeeding, speech and quality-of-life outcomes.  A prospective cohort of 37 children who had CO2 laser frenectomy plus myofunctional exercises reported improvements in speech in 89%, along with feeding and sleep outcomes, using parent questionnaires. [5]

A case report and systematic review described major complications after tongue-tie release and noted that complications are thought to be low but are not well reported or studied; it also reported a more than tenfold increase in diagnoses and frenotomies in the US from 1997 to 2012. [6] Wikipedia mentions post-operative pain in some adults, an uncited claim. [3] Myofunctional therapy is discussed in the literature as an adjunct to reduce tissue reattachment.

timeline.event: Reported over tenfold rise in tongue-tie diagnoses and frenotomies in the US. [6]
Structured review on tongue-tie and breastfeeding published. [2]
